advanced_buying.title: Procurement 8 — Advanced Buying: Settings, Scorecards & Structure
advanced_buying.desc: The structural layer: Buying Settings as the constitution, the PO/PR enforcement pair, the supplier scorecard fed by the whole track, subcontracting, the analytics layer, the purchasing calendar, and roles and delegation — closing the track's eighth law.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Buying Settings: the defaults that govern
lessons.html:
Selling 8 opened with the settings philosophy, and it transfers whole: defaults are policy — every choice a document makes without asking a human was made once, here, and the consultant who configures this screen is writing the client's buying constitution. The buy-side counterpart is Buying Settings, and its handful of fields deserve the same deliberate hour.

  • Supplier naming — by name or by series (SUP-00001): the identity convention for the entire supply base, chosen ONCE at implementation. Naming-by-name reads humanly everywhere (lists, ledgers, reports) and suits the trading firms you serve; series suits scale and homonym-heavy bases. The unglamorous truth from Selling 8 applies verbatim: changing convention mid-life is a migration, not a setting — choose at the start, deliberately.
  • Default buying price list — the list documents reach for when no supplier-scoped price answers (Procurement 2's hierarchy needs its floor named here).
  • The over-receipt allowance, global — the fallback tolerance where the item sets none (Procurement 6's gate rule needs its default written somewhere, and this is where). The posture transfers: a small deliberate number for bulk-tolerant trade, zero where identity classes dominate — and per-item overrides carrying the exceptions.
  • Maintain same rate throughout the purchase cycle — the toggle that REFUSES rate divergence between a PO and the receipts and invoices made from it. Understand what it enforces before touching it: this is the rate-amendment conviction (Procurement 5) and the price-variance match (Procurement 7) expressed as configuration — with it on, the committed rate travels untouched and deviations must confront the match; with it off, rates drift per document and the match inherits noise. For trading clients the answer is almost always ON, and turning it off to make an error message go away is Chapter 9's first pattern.

The configuration conversation. As with selling: the settings hour happens WITH the client's owner and accountant, each toggle read as the policy question it is (may receipts exceed orders, and by how much? may rates change mid-cycle? must purchases begin with orders? — the next chapter's pair), the answers written into the implementation record. A firm that cannot answer these questions in words is not ready to answer them in configuration — and discovering that IS the consultation. Write the answers down; the next two chapters enforce them.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The enforcement pair: PO Required & PR Required
lessons.html:
Two toggles in Buying Settings carry more governance weight than everything else on the screen combined, because they decide whether this track's document chain is a RECOMMENDATION or a LAW.

Purchase Order Required. ON: no Purchase Receipt or Purchase Invoice stands without a PO behind it — the commitment layer (Procurement 5) becomes mandatory, the unordered truck (Procurement 6) loses its last loophole, and the standalone invoice (Procurement 7's suspicion) is refused at the root. OFF: documents may begin anywhere, and the chain holds only by training and habit.

Purchase Receipt Required. ON: no Purchase Invoice books without possession recorded — the three-way match's physical leg (Procurement 6-7) becomes structural: paying for goods the firm cannot show becomes not merely convicted but IMPOSSIBLE in the ordinary course. OFF: invoices may book direct, and the match runs only where receipts happen to exist.

The judgment — enforcement is sized, not assumed. The reflex answer (both ON, everywhere) is usually right for goods trade and wrong as a reflex. The honest configuration walks the firm's spend: stock purchases — both ON, no exceptions worth having; services — a receipt of possession is often meaningless (there is no truck), so the service categories bill against POs without PRs, per policy; the exempted tail — utilities, statutory payments, the small direct spend Procurement 3's proportionality already excused. The system honours this judgment per item and category where configuration allows, and by written policy where it does not — the point being that EXCEPTIONS ARE DESIGNED, not discovered: the firm decides where the chain binds, writes it down, and the toggles enforce the decision rather than a blanket.

What enforcement changes, in operating terms. With the pair ON for stock trade: maverick buying is not a report finding but a refused save; the match queue is complete by construction (every invoice has its receipt, every receipt its order); and the audit's chain-of-custody question is answered by the system's own refusal to have allowed anything else. The support tickets change character too — from why do the numbers disagree (archaeology) to the system will not let me book this (a policy conversation with the answer already written). The second ticket is the cheap one, and buying it deliberately is what this pair is for.

The override discipline. Genuine exceptions arise (the emergency the policy foresaw); the lawful path is role-gated permission to proceed with a reason logged — never the toggle flipped OFF temporarily, which repeals the constitution to answer one letter. The quarterly exceptions read (Procurement 4's governance) is where the overrides are counted, and a rising count is the policy asking to be rewritten honestly — either the chain binds or it does not, but it never merely erodes.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The supplier scorecard: the track's data, weaponised
lessons.html:
Every module of this track has been quietly generating supplier evidence: committed dates and their slips (Procurement 5), rejections by reason (Procurement 6), match variances and payment behaviour (Procurement 7). The supplier scorecard is where the evidence becomes an instrument — a standing, periodic score per supplier that the relationship is then MANAGED by.

What feeds it. The scorecard evaluates each supplier per period (monthly or quarterly are the working rhythms) across weighted criteria the firm declares: delivery performance — OTIF against the supplier's own committed dates, computable because Procurement 5 recorded honestly; quality — rejection rate at the gate, by quantity or by lots, flowing from Procurement 6's fork; commercial conduct — invoice accuracy (the match's variance log), price stability against agreed rates, responsiveness where the firm chooses to score it. The weights are the firm's values written as arithmetic — the pharma distributor weights quality above all; the fast-retail chain weights OTIF — and the Procurement 4 rule governs here too: weights declared before the period, never adjusted after to produce a preferred verdict.

What the score DOES. A scorecard that only reports is a newsletter. The instrument's teeth are its standings and their consequences: the standing bands (the names vary — what matters is the ladder) mapping to ACTIONS — the top band earns preference in sourcing and the terms-extension conversations; the middle earns the ordinary course; the warning band triggers the documented conversation with a review date; and the bottom triggers the hold machinery (Procurement 1's types — new RFQs suspended, or new POs suspended, per the firm's escalation). Where configuration supports automatic consequences (warnings raised on new documents to poorly-standing suppliers, or prevention outright), the automation enforces what the review decided — the score decides nothing alone; it ARMS the decision.

The quarterly review, transformed. Procurement 1 promised reviews conducted from records; the scorecard is the record, pre-assembled. The Emzor conversation opens with the period's numbers — OTIF, rejections, match record — and both sides argue from the same page: praise is specific (96%, thank you), problems are specific (the transit-damage trend is a haulier conversation, and here are the receipts), and the supplier's own data requests are answerable. Suppliers learn quickly that this customer's memory is written — and their conduct prices it in, which is the scorecard's quiet second function: it improves suppliers who never see it.

The fairness disciplines. Score against commitments, not wishes (OTIF to THEIR date — the Procurement 5 rule); score what the supplier controls (your own late payments distorting their behaviour is your finding, not theirs); review the criteria annually (a scorecard measuring what stopped mattering manages toward the wrong supplier); and share the framework with key suppliers openly — a supplier who knows the rules plays to them, and the ones who object to being measured have told you something worth scoring.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Subcontracting: your materials, their work
lessons.html:
A flow every Nigerian trading-adjacent firm eventually meets: you supply the materials; an outside party does the work; finished goods come back. The repackaging house that turns your bulk into retail packs, the toll processor, the contract manufacturer running your brand. Subcontracting is its own machinery, and this chapter is the working overview a consultant needs — where the boundary of this track sits, and what lies past it.

The shape of the flow. A subcontracted purchase order names the SERVICE being bought (the processing, per unit of output) and the finished item expected back; against it, YOUR materials transfer OUT to the subcontractor — leaving your warehouse but not your OWNERSHIP: they sit in a supplier-side warehouse of yours, visible, valued, yours — and the finished goods return on receipt, consuming the transferred materials per the recipe and carrying a cost built from your materials plus their service charge. One flow, three truths kept simultaneously: the materials never stopped being yours; the service is the only thing purchased; the finished cost is honest arithmetic, not the subcontractor's invoice alone.

Why the machinery matters — the failure it replaces. The informal version: materials sent on a waybill and goodwill, finished goods received as if purchased outright, the subcontractor's invoice booked whole. Three lies at once — stock vanished that was never consumed (the sent materials evaporate from the ledger), cost doubled (materials expensed at exit AND inside the finished price), and the exposure invisible (how much of OUR stock sits at THEIR site is a question with no answer). The formal flow keeps the answer live: the supplier-side stock view is the exposure report, reconciled like any warehouse — because that is what it is.

The operating disciplines, familiar by design. Every rule this track taught applies with the names changed: the transfer out is a documented movement (Procurement 3's discipline); the recipe (materials-per-finished-unit) is a master someone owns, and variance against it — the subcontractor consuming more than the recipe says — is the scrap/yield conversation, held from records; the return gate counts, captures identities, and forks rejects exactly as Procurement 6 taught (the repacker's output carries YOUR batch obligations); and the service invoice matches against the subcontract PO and the received output — the three-way match with a recipe inside it. Periodic reconciliation of the supplier-side warehouse against the subcontractor's own count closes the loop — the statement reconciliation's physical twin.

The consultant's boundary. Where subcontracting deepens — multi-level recipes, scrap accounting, work-in-progress valuation — the terrain belongs to the manufacturing curriculum, and the honest consultant names the boundary rather than improvising across it. What this track equips you to do: recognise the flow when a client describes it (we send them our sugar and buy back the packed sachets is a subcontract, whatever they call it), set up the simple version soundly, and know which specialist conversation the complex version deserves.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The analytics layer: reading the buying function
lessons.html:
Selling 8 closed with reports as the discipline of reading; procurement's shelf is the mirror, and by now every report on it is just a module of this track viewed from above. The layer, organised by the question each report answers:

  • What are we spending, and where? Purchase analytics — spend by supplier, by item group, by period: the concentration read (Procurement 1's tree, quantified — the top-five share, watched), the category trends, the volume evidence that opens every terms renegotiation. This is the report the MD reads monthly, and its first service is surprise-prevention: the category that doubled quietly, the supplier who became a dependency without a decision.
  • Are we paying the right prices? The price-trend read per item per supplier: last-paid against agreed rates (Procurement 2's drift eye, systematised), rate movements across the year, the loyalty-tax audit that feeds the market-test calendar (Procurement 4). One page per key item answers the question every owner asks eventually — are we buying well? — with a line instead of a feeling.
  • Is the pipeline healthy? The open-PO views by status and expected date (Procurement 5's worklists, aggregated): committed-and-undelivered by supplier and age, the sweep's candidate list, the receiving forecast. The inbound backlog is a number treasury and sales both plan against, and this shelf is where it lives.
  • Is the gate holding? Receiving and quality reads — rejection rates by supplier and reason, quarantine aging, inspection outcomes (Procurement 6's evidence, trended). Feeding the scorecard, and read on its own for the process question: a rejection rate falling toward zero is either quality improving or the fork rusting, and the quarantine-aging line says which.
  • Is the money right? AP aging and its discipline (Procurement 7), the match's variance log (the overcharge-attempt trend by supplier — a civility index of your supply base), WHT payable reconciliation state, input-VAT capture completeness. The finance shelf, read weekly at the run and monthly at the close.

The cadence, not the catalogue. The Selling 8 rule transfers verbatim: reports serve decisions, and each earns its rhythm — daily (the queue, the match queue, expected arrivals), weekly (the run's selection, the sweep, quarantine), monthly (spend analytics, statement recs, the two tax reconciliations), quarterly (scorecards, market tests, the exceptions read). A report nobody acts on is decoration; the analytics layer is exactly as valuable as the calendar that reads it — which is the next chapter.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The purchasing calendar: every rhythm, one page
lessons.html:
Eight modules have each installed rhythms; scattered, they are good intentions — assembled, they are an operating system. This chapter is the consolidation: the procurement function's recurring work, one page, with owners.

Daily — the queues. The request queue reviewed (new demand judged, auto-triggers released, consolidation candidates flagged — Procurement 3); the match queue worked oldest-first (Procurement 7); today's expected arrivals confirmed against the dock plan (Procurement 5-6). Fifteen focused minutes each; the difference between a function that runs and one that reacts.

Weekly — the run and the sweeps. The payment run — selection, verification, approval, execution, advices (Procurement 7's full ceremony); the quarantine review (Procurement 6 — what is here, why, whose next step); the unacknowledged-PO chase and the expediting pass over the late list (Procurement 5). The week's shape: money out on schedule, exceptions aging nowhere.

Monthly — the reconciliations and the truths. Supplier statement reconciliations for the majors (Procurement 1 — where your debit notes meet their credit notes); the phantom-incoming sweep of stale POs (Procurement 5); the unallocated-advances read, both directions (Procurement 7); WHT payable reconciled and REMITTED on the statutory date; input and output VAT reconciled to their registers before the 21st; spend analytics to the MD (Chapter 5). The month's discipline is what makes the year's audit boring.

Quarterly — the reviews and the tests. Scorecards computed and the supplier reviews held from them (Chapter 3); the market tests the calendar owes this quarter (Procurement 4's rotation); the exceptions read — single-source purchases, override counts, direct-entry share (Procurement 2-4's governance instruments, read together); the planning-fields exception review — stockouts and never-turns tuning reorder levels and lead times (Procurement 2-3).

Annually — the constitution reviewed. Terms renegotiations from the year's payment record (Procurement 1's extension path, argued from AP evidence); the scorecard criteria themselves reviewed (Chapter 3's fairness rule); the settings walked again with the owner (Chapters 1-2 — the firm changed this year; did its constitution keep up?); the supply-base pruning — dormant suppliers disabled, the tree's shape re-read against strategy.

The calendar's owner. A rhythm without a name attached is a hope. The implementation deliverable is this page WITH the names filled in — who runs the queue, who prepares the run, who releases it, who holds the Emzor review — sized to the firm: in the 11-person company several names are the same person, and the calendar is precisely how that person eventually delegates without losing the function (the next chapter's subject). The consultant who leaves a client with configured software has done half the job; the calendar with owners is the other half.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Roles, separation & the function that outlives its founder
lessons.html:
Procurement concentrates the firm's money-out authority, which makes its role design a control question BEFORE it is an org-chart question. This chapter is the separation logic, sized honestly from eleven people to a hundred.

The three authorities, named. Across this track, three distinct powers have been exercised: committing (raising and approving POs — deciding what is bought, from whom, at what rate), possessing (receiving — deciding what physically enters and what the count says), and paying (booking invoices and releasing the run — deciding what money leaves). The control principle is that these authorities CHECK each other — the three-way match is literally the three authorities' documents held against one another — and separation is what keeps the check real: the person who commits should not be the person who single-handedly pays; the person who receives should not approve their own variances. Collusion-resistant is the standard; friction-free is not the goal.

Sized to eleven people. The small firm cannot staff three departments, and does not need to — it needs the AUTHORITIES separated even where hats share heads: the buyer raises, the owner or a second signer approves above threshold; whoever receives is not the same person booking that receipt's invoice unchecked; the run is prepared by one and released by another (Procurement 7's minimum, restated as the irreducible core). Two people can hold a sound control set if the two are chosen deliberately; what cannot hold it is one person with every authority and no review — which is not an insult to the person but a description of what fraud investigators call opportunity, and what auditors call a finding.

The permissions posture. Roles in the system mirror the design: creation rights, approval thresholds, the release permission, master-data amendment rights (the supplier's bank details being the crown jewels — Procurement 1's out-of-band rule needs its edit permission held tightly), and the settings themselves (Chapters 1-2) behind the narrowest door of all. The Selling 8 principle transfers: permissions enforce the design; they do not substitute for having one.

The founder-as-bottleneck, buy-side. The pattern every growing firm hits: procurement lives in the founder's head — the supplier relationships, the fair prices, the who-to-call — and every order waits on one person's attention. This track, read as a whole, IS the delegation instrument: the masters hold the relationships (Procurement 1), the rates (2), the demand logic (3), the sourcing files (4); the documents hold the commitments and their states (5-7); the calendar holds the rhythm (Chapter 6); the scorecard holds the judgment's evidence (3). What the founder then delegates is not trust in a person's memory but OPERATION of a system that remembers — the difference between hoping a hire is honest and knowing the structure would notice. The handover test is concrete: could a competent newcomer, given the masters, the files, and the calendar, run purchasing for a month without a single question answerable only by the founder? Every NO in that sentence is a module of this track not yet done properly — which makes the test both the goal and the audit.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's procurement year
lessons.html:
The threads of six modules, run for four quarters. The last case study reads the function operating as a system — each beat naming its chapter.

Q1 — the constitution hardened (Ch. 1-2). The settings hour, held properly this time after a near-miss: a services invoice had booked standalone against a supplier with no PO anywhere — caught by the match queue's completeness check, harmless, instructive. The walk with the MD and accountant lands: PO Required ON for all stock categories; PR Required ON likewise; the services list written (clearing, haulage, professional fees — PO yes, PR no); the exempted tail named (utilities, statutory); over-receipt at 2% global, zero on serialized; maintain-same-rate ON. The override permission sits with the MD alone, reason-logged. Two support tickets the following week say the system will not let me — both answered by pointing at the written policy. The constitution holds.

Q2 — the scorecard's first full quarter (Ch. 3). Weights declared in advance: quality 40, OTIF 35, commercial 25 — pharma's values as arithmetic. The quarter computes: Emzor lands mid-band — OTIF 91% (the allocation short-close remembered honestly), rejections 1.7% (the transit-damage trend), match record clean. The review opens with the numbers; Emzor's rep arrives with their own copy (the framework was shared — Ch. 3's openness rule); the haulier conversation produces a packaging change; the backup distributor's clean quarter earns them a standing second-source slice (Procurement 4's split logic, now scorecard-armed). The suppliers' conduct across Q3 prices in the fact that this customer's memory is written.

Q3 — the subcontract (Ch. 4). A retail chain wants HealthTrade's paracetamol in blister-strip singles. The repackaging house is onboarded through the full gate (NAFDAC provenance obligations riding the output); the subcontract PO names the service per thousand strips; bulk cartons transfer OUT — visible in the supplier-side warehouse, still HealthTrade's stock; finished strips return through the counting, batch-capturing, fork-ready gate; the service invoice matches PO-and-output. Month two's reconciliation catches a yield variance — the repacker consuming 3% over recipe — and the conversation happens from records, settling on a revised recipe and a scrap allowance. The exposure question (how much of our stock sits at their site?) is a live number all quarter.

Q4 — the calendar closes its year (Ch. 5-7). The annual beats run: terms renegotiation with the backup distributor argued from four quarters of on-time runs — Net-15 becomes Net-30; the Emzor market test (calendar-owed) re-competes the paracetamol rate — Emzor retains at a 2% sharpening, the file refreshed, the loyalty tax audited to zero; the settings walk finds one change (a new serialized category zeroes its tolerance); the supply base prunes four dormant suppliers to disabled. And the year's quiet milestone (Ch. 7): the founder takes three weeks out of the country; purchasing runs on the calendar, the masters, and the two-signature run — twenty-one days, zero questions only she could answer. The handover test, passed in production.

The year's one page (Ch. 5). Spend concentration: top five suppliers at 61%, watched, deliberate. Price drift on key items: within agreed rates, two renegotiations banked. Match log: ₦340k of attempted overcharges stopped across the year, at the cost of eleven emails. Rejection trend: falling, with the fork demonstrably in use. WHT remitted on schedule all twelve months; both VAT accounts reconciling in the hour they should. The buying function, read from one page — which is the point of everything this track has built.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Patterns, the eighth law & the track complete
lessons.html:
The advanced layer's scar tissue, then the law that closes the track.

Pattern 1 — "the setting was blocking us, so we turned it off." Disease: the constitution repealed to answer one letter (Ch. 1-2) — maintain-same-rate off to silence a variance, PO-required off for one urgent booking, and the protections gone for everyone thereafter. Fix: the override path (role-gated, reason-logged) exists precisely so the toggle never moves; a setting that keeps blocking honest work is retuned deliberately in the settings walk, not disabled in the corridor.

Pattern 2 — "the scorecard says whatever the review wants it to say." Disease: weights adjusted after the period, criteria bent per supplier (Ch. 3) — the instrument now launders preference as measurement. Fix: weights declared in advance and changed only at the annual criteria review; overrides of the score's implication written with reasons — judgment above the arithmetic is legitimate; arithmetic bent beneath the judgment is not.

Pattern 3 — "we do not know how much of our stock is at the subcontractor." Disease: the informal toll flow (Ch. 4) — materials on waybills and goodwill, ownership evaporated from the ledger. Fix: the formal flow's three truths restored — transfer to the supplier-side warehouse, recipe-governed consumption, cost built honestly — and the periodic physical reconciliation that keeps the exposure a number.

Pattern 4 — "the reports exist; nobody reads them." Disease: analytics as decoration (Ch. 5) — the shelf built, the calendar absent. Fix: each report bound to its decision and its rhythm with an owner; the unread report retired honestly (a smaller read shelf beats a larger ignored one).

Pattern 5 — "everything still waits for one person." Disease: the bottleneck unrelieved (Ch. 7) — the system built and the delegation never made, authority hoarded past the structure that would hold it. Fix: the handover test run honestly, its NOs converted module by module — and the three-week absence attempted deliberately before it is imposed by circumstance.

The eighth law. The seven so far: purchase documents are downstream of supplier masters; cost truth begins at the item; the request layer separates need from commitment; sourcing is a decision record; the PO is the single source of inbound truth; the receiving gate is where the world enters the system; the purchase ledger is the spend truth. The eighth closes the arc exactly as Selling's did, because it is the same truth facing the other way: buying that lives in masters, documents, and rhythms — not in anyone's head — is the buying function that survives growth, turnover, and the founder's absence. Settings are the constitution; the scorecard is memory with teeth; the calendar is the function's heartbeat; and separation of authority is what lets trust be structural instead of personal.

The track, complete. Eight modules, one arc: the supply base built and governed (1), the item architecture that makes cost true (2), demand made visible and governable (3), sourcing made a record (4), commitment made single-source truth (5), the gate made honest (6), the money made matched, taxed, and controlled (7), and the whole made structure (8). Read backward, every module was building the three-way match and the handover test; read forward, a consultant who holds all eight can walk into any Nigerian trading firm and see, within a day, which laws are kept, which are broken, and what each break is costing — which is precisely the professional this certification exists to produce. Take the assessments; then go find the breaks.
